prompt:
Write a technical description of about 1,000 words of what happens between a browser being given an HTTPS address and the first byte of the response arriving. The reader is a junior web developer.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Write mostly medium-length, complete sentences.
context_note: Prompt sent as the subagent's whole task. The subagent also carried the Claude Code agent system prompt, tool definitions and CLAUDE.md.
sampling: harness defaults; not set by the experimenter
text:
When you type an HTTPS address into a browser and press Enter, the first thing the browser does is work out what you actually asked for. It parses the address into a scheme, a host name, an optional port, a path, and any query string or fragment, and it notes that the scheme is https, which means the connection must be encrypted and the default port is 443. Before touching the network, the browser checks several local sources. It may consult a list of sites that must only ever be reached over HTTPS, it looks in its HTTP cache to see whether a fresh copy of the resource is already stored, and it may find that a service worker registered by the site wants to answer the request itself. If none of those can satisfy the request, the browser has to go out and fetch the page.

The next job is to turn the host name into an IP address, because networks route packets by number rather than by name. The browser first checks its own DNS cache, then asks the operating system, which checks its own cache and the hosts file. If neither knows the answer, the request goes to a recursive resolver, usually run by your internet provider or a public service. That resolver, if it has no cached answer, walks the hierarchy of the domain system: it asks a root server which servers handle the top-level domain such as .com, asks those which servers are authoritative for the domain, and finally asks the authoritative server for the address records. Each answer carries a time-to-live value that tells every cache along the way how long it may reuse the result, which is why a DNS change can take a while to be seen everywhere. Modern browsers often ask for both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses and may also look up newer record types that advertise supported protocols, and many can send these queries over an encrypted channel so that the network cannot easily read them.

With an address in hand, the browser opens a connection to the server. For classic HTTPS this is a TCP connection, which begins with a three-step handshake. The browser sends a SYN packet, the server answers with a SYN-ACK, and the browser replies with an ACK, after which both sides have agreed on starting sequence numbers and can send data reliably and in order. This costs one full round trip between you and the server, so physical distance matters here, and it is one reason content delivery networks place servers close to users. If several addresses are available, the browser may race connections to different ones and keep whichever completes first, which helps when one network path is slow or broken.

Once TCP is established, the browser and server perform a TLS handshake to set up encryption and to prove the server is who it claims to be. The browser opens with a message that lists the TLS versions and cipher suites it supports, includes a random value, and sends a key share for an ephemeral Diffie-Hellman exchange. It also includes the server name indication, which tells the server which host name the client wants, so that one machine can serve many sites with different certificates. In TLS 1.3 the server responds in a single flight with its own key share, its certificate chain, and a signature proving it holds the private key matching that certificate. From the two key shares, both sides independently compute the same shared secret without ever sending it, and from that they derive the symmetric keys used to encrypt everything that follows. Because the key exchange is ephemeral, recording the traffic today does not let an attacker decrypt it later even if the server's long-term key is stolen.

Verification of the certificate happens in parallel with this. The browser checks that the certificate chain leads up to a certificate authority it already trusts, that every certificate in the chain is within its validity dates, that the host name you requested appears in the certificate's subject alternative names, and that the certificate has not been revoked, which it may determine from a stapled response supplied by the server or from locally distributed revocation data. If any of these checks fails, the browser stops and shows a warning page rather than continuing, because without them encryption would protect you only from eavesdroppers and not from an impostor. With TLS 1.3 the handshake needs one additional round trip after TCP, and when you have visited the site before, session resumption can shorten it further, sometimes allowing the browser to send encrypted data in its very first message.

Newer deployments may skip much of this sequence. HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, which uses UDP and folds the transport and encryption handshakes into one, so a new connection costs a single round trip instead of two or three. Browsers learn that a site supports it from an Alt-Svc header on an earlier response or from a DNS record, and they often fall back to TCP if UDP is blocked. If the browser already has an open connection to the same server, particularly with HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, it can reuse that connection and skip the handshakes entirely.

Now the browser finally sends the HTTP request itself, encrypted inside the TLS session. It consists of a method such as GET, the path and query, and a set of headers including the Host or authority, the Accept headers describing the content types and encodings it understands, the User-Agent, and any cookies stored for that site. Under HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 this is sent as compressed binary frames, but the meaning is the same. The request may first pass through a load balancer, reverse proxy, or CDN edge, which terminates TLS, picks a backend, and may answer from its own cache. The application server then routes the request, runs whatever code and database queries are needed, and begins writing a response.

The moment the first byte of that response travels back across the network and reaches the browser is what performance tools call time to first byte. It is the sum of everything described above: name lookup, connection setup, encryption setup, request transit, server processing, and the return trip. Knowing where that time goes is the first step in making a site load faster.
